issues.description: The procedure states that participants chose their own conditions rather than being randomly assigned. Self-selection into intervention and identifiability conditions fundamentally undermines causal inference, introduces selection confounds, and deviates from the original study's random assignment. This is the single most damaging threat to internal validity in the replication and would invalidate any comparison of condition means.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The design is described as 'within-subject,' but the original studies were between-subjects, the analyses use between-subjects ANOVAs, and the descriptive tables report separate (non-overlapping) sample sizes for each cell (e.g., 159, 175, 166). A within-subjects design would require every participant to experience multiple conditions and would change the appropriate error terms and power calculations. This contradiction makes the actual design unclear and the analytic approach potentially mis-specified.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively.

issues.description: The original effect concerned real donations of actual money (five one-dollar bills earned in a prior task). The replication substitutes a hypothetical/imaginary donation with no real stakes and removes the earned-money manipulation. Hypothetical generosity is known to diverge from real prosocial behavior, so this change may eliminate or alter the very phenomenon being tested, threatening the construct validity of the replication.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: power analysis based on inflated effect
issues.description: Sample size and evaluation are benchmarked against the original Study 1 effect (d = 0.48), but the manuscript itself notes that the meta-analytic estimate of the identifiable victim effect is only 0.05. Powering to the original, likely inflated, effect rather than to a more realistic meta-analytic estimate risks an underpowered design for the true effect size and biases the replication evaluation.
issues.quote: comparing the replication effect with the original effect (d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.11, 0.84]) obtained from the power analysis using the criteria set by Lebel, Vanpaemel, Cheung, and Campbell (2019)

issues.description: The power analysis description is circular and contains no actual numbers (target effect size, alpha, power, or resulting N). The reader cannot evaluate whether the sample is adequately powered. The placeholder/duplicated sentence ('To obtain the minimal sample size required for this study, The sample size for this study was determined...') compounds the lack of detail.
issues.quote: To obtain the minimal sample size required for this study, The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study.

issues.description: The (placeholder) result shows participants donating MORE to statistical victims than to identifiable victims — the opposite of the identifiable victim effect being tested. The text reports this as a significant 'finding' without noting it directly contradicts the hypothesized direction. If this pattern arose in real data, treating a reversed effect as confirmation of an 'identifiability effect' would be a serious interpretive error.
issues.quote: meaning that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: internal inconsistency between tables and text
issues.description: The post-hoc text labels the statistical-victim condition as having the higher mean (M=2.54) and the identifiable-victim condition the lower (M=2.24), but the descriptive statistics in Table 7 imply the reverse (identifiable combined ≈2.54; statistical combined ≈2.25). The condition labels appear swapped, making it impossible to know which group actually donated more. Such inconsistencies undermine confidence in the reported analyses.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)

issues.description: Several 'significant' post-hoc contrasts report effect-size confidence intervals that include zero. For example, Identifiable vs Statistical shows d=0.076, 95% CI [-0.05, 0.20], yet pBonferroni=.049; similarly Statistical vs Joint shows d=0.08, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.23], p=.041. A CI spanning zero is logically incompatible with a significant difference at the same alpha, indicating an error in computation or reporting.

The abstract claims the extension hypothesis was supported, but Hypothesis 6 predicted that identifiable victims elicit HIGHER perceived impact than statistical victims, whereas the results show no identifiable-vs-statistical difference and a statistical>joint difference. The abstract's claim does not match either the hypothesis or the reported results (and is based on random dummy data). This risks misleading readers about what was found.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: Although the dataset is acknowledged as a Qualtrics-generated placeholder, the reported demographics are implausible for an MTurk sample (mean age 67.8, SD 30.1, range 18–120). An age of 120 is impossible and a mean near 68 is inconsistent with typical MTurk samples. This signals that the planned data-quality checks (e.g., implausible-age screening) and exclusion criteria need to be specified before real data collection.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.description: Multiple distinct affective/moral items are combined into a single 'aggregated feeling' variable, but no internal-consistency statistic (e.g., Cronbach's alpha) or factor-analytic justification is reported for aggregating heterogeneous items (upset, touched, sympathy, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, perceived impact). Without demonstrated reliability/unidimensionality, the aggregate may be psychometrically invalid.
issues.quote: Identifiability and intervention on aggregated feelings  Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.description: The segregated-feelings analysis tests six dependent variables across three effects (18 ANOVA tests) plus numerous post-hoc contrasts, but no family-wise correction is applied across this set. The single 'significant' perceived-impact result (p=.045) is borderline and likely a false positive given the number of tests, especially with random data.
issues.quote: only the result of identifiability on the perceived impact of donation yielded significant findings.

issues.description: Perceived impact is repeatedly framed as a mediator of the identifiable victim effect, but the analysis plan only includes group-mean comparisons and correlations, not a mediation model. The mismatch between the theoretical framing ('mediation effect of perceived impact') and the planned analyses means the extension cannot actually test the proposed mechanism.
issues.quote: Yet, there were mixed findings regarding the mediation effect of perceived impact on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.description: To merge Studies 1 and 3, the explicit intervention is now also applied to the joint condition, which was not done in the original. While framed as enabling comparison, this changes the original design and adds conditions not present in the source, complicating direct comparison to the original effects and the interpretation of the 'implicit' manipulation.
issues.quote: The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.description: The key independent variable is the induction of deliberative/analytical thinking, yet no manipulation check is described to verify that the intervention actually increased deliberative processing. Without such a check, a null result cannot distinguish between a failed manipulation and a genuine absence of the effect.
issues.quote: thinking analytically about your helping behaviour would reduce your motivation to offer assistance to a single beneficiary

issues.description: In the original, participants donated money they had earned in a prior task, creating genuine opportunity cost. Removing the pre-survey earning step eliminates the sense of giving up one's own money, which may substantially weaken the affective/deliberative dynamics central to the effect. This deviation is more than 'minor.'
issues.quote: Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.description: Moving from a controlled laboratory with face-to-face charity request to an anonymous online MTurk survey changes social presence, attentiveness, and the salience of the donation act—factors plausibly central to sympathy-driven giving. Combined with hypothetical donations, the cumulative deviations may move this beyond a 'close to very close' replication.
issues.quote: Online survey Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.description: The large N (~1000) yields 'significant' p-values for effects that are practically negligible (e.g., identifiability ηp2 = .007). The manuscript reports these as supported effects without discussing that the effect sizes are far below the original (ηp2 ≈ .06) and trivial in magnitude. Interpreting tiny effects as confirmation conflates statistical and practical significance.

Post-hoc tables report a negative t-statistic alongside a positive Cohen's d for the same contrast (e.g., t=-2.40 with d=0.076), and elsewhere mix signs without a clear convention. Inconsistent sign reporting makes the direction of effects ambiguous and hampers interpretation and replication checking.

issues.subcategory: exclusion criteria not reconciled with N
issues.description: The text states that participants with prior knowledge of the effect and those failing attention checks were excluded, yet the analyzed N remains exactly 1000 with no exclusion counts reported. The handling and reporting of exclusions (and resulting final N per cell) need to be specified to assess data quality and avoid undisclosed flexibility.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The key author 'Slovic' is repeatedly misspelled as 'Solvic' in the text, and the reference list contains duplicated/garbled entries. While minor, such errors in a replication report—particularly of the target article's author—undermine confidence in care taken with the literature and citations.
issues.quote: Solvic (2007) argued for the drawbacks of the phenomenon to raise awareness on our indifference of numerous death in genocide.

issues.description: The 'perceived impact of donation' extension item is added into the same aggregated-feelings composite used to compare against the original, while also being analyzed separately. Including a novel extension item in the aggregate that is meant to mirror the original measure makes the replication's aggregate non-comparable to the original study's feeling composite.
issues.quote: Note: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)
